summary: Engines can ice up in three ways: carburettor ice (fuel evaporating chills the carb by up to 35°C), impact ice on the intake or filter, and ice or water in the fuel system. Carb ice can form on a warm humid day, not just a cold one. Use carb heat for at least 15 seconds, apply it before reducing power, and always follow the AFM. Built from CAA Safety Sense Leaflet 14, not yet from your own notes.
src: Safety Sense Leaflet 14: Piston Engine Icing
sections: Three types of engine icing
Carburettor ice: fuel evaporating in the venturi cools the carb by up to 35°C below the outside air. Water vapour freezes and chokes the venturi and throttle. Fuel-injected engines do not get it
Impact (intake) ice: ice builds on or in the air intake or blocks the filter. Needs visible moisture below 0°C, and affects carburettor and injected engines alike
Fuel system ice: water in tanks or lines freezes, often at bends or filters. Water can stop an engine even if it never freezes
Car fuel (MOGAS) may be more prone to water problems than AVGAS
When it happens
Carb icing is possible on warm days, not only in the cold. Worst band is roughly 0°C to 10°C with high humidity
Tests showed serious ice at descent power with air above 25°C and humidity as low as 30%
Clues for high humidity: temperature and dew point close together, wet ground, rain, fog or low cloud
Descent power carries the greatest risk of serious carb ice
Recognising it
First sign is usually a loss of power or performance
Fixed-pitch prop: a small RPM drop with falling airspeed or height. Opening the throttle slightly can hide it
Constant-speed prop: manifold pressure drops first while RPM stays steady
With an autopilot holding height, airspeed can quietly decay, so watch it
An EGT gauge often shows a drop before power is lost
Fuel icing: power loss in cold, clear air where carb ice is not the cause
Using carb heat and alternate air
Carb heat sends air through an exhaust heat exchanger and bypasses the filter. A small power drop when selected is normal
Alternate air (injected engines) bypasses a blocked intake or filter. Apply it fully on, and keep it on until clear of icing and the ice has melted
Select heat for at least 15 seconds. Rough running at first is normal as ice melts: keep heat on
If the engine fails and carb ice is suspected, keep heat hot as residual exhaust warmth may allow a restart
Always follow the AFM. Do not use continuous carb heat at high power unless the AFM allows it
Procedures by phase of flight
Start and taxi: start with heat cold. Avoid heat when taxiing because the air is unfiltered
Power checks: heat fully on for 15 seconds. A typical drop is 75 to 100 RPM or 3 to 5 inches of MP. If power rises above the earlier value when heat goes off, ice was present: repeat until clear
Take-off: normally heat cold. If a long time passed since the checks, apply about 15 seconds just before
Cruise: monitor RPM or MP and apply heat periodically in conducive conditions
Descent: apply heat before reducing power and add power regularly to keep the engine warm
Landing: heat on downwind, and many types go cold at around 300 ft ready for a go-around
Go-around: check carb heat is cold before and after applying power
Prevention on the ground
Keep tanks full to reduce condensation, including in a hangar
Check fuel for water and check filler cap seals for deterioration
Take extra care with MOGAS and barrel fuel
Periodically check the carb heat or alternate air controls and seals

sum.Three types of engine icing: Carburettor, intake and fuel system ice, and which engines they affect.
sum.When it happens: Humid air between 0°C and 10°C is worst, but warm days can ice too.
sum.Recognising it: Power loss shows as RPM or manifold pressure falling first.
sum.Using carb heat and alternate air: Select heat for at least 15 seconds and expect rough running as it clears.
sum.Procedures by phase of flight: Heat on before power off in descent, cold again for the go-around.
sum.Prevention on the ground: Full tanks, drained water checks and good seals.

cards.q: What cools the carburettor enough to cause ice?
cards.a: Fuel evaporating in the venturi, up to 35°C below the outside air.

cards.q: Which engines cannot get carb ice?
cards.a: Fuel-injected engines. They can still get intake (impact) ice.

cards.q: Temperature band with the highest carb ice risk in humid air?
cards.a: About 0°C to 10°C, but it can happen on warm days too.

cards.q: First sign of carb ice in a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft?
cards.a: A small RPM drop with falling airspeed or height.

cards.q: First sign of carb ice with a constant-speed propeller?
cards.a: Manifold pressure falls while RPM stays the same.

cards.q: How long should carb heat be selected to clear ice?
Normal power-check drop with carb heat on?
cards.a: About 75 to 100 RPM or 3 to 5 inches of MP.

cards.q: When should carb heat be applied during a descent?
cards.a: Before reducing power, then keep adding power regularly.

cards.q: Why avoid carb heat while taxiing?
cards.a: Heated air bypasses the filter, so it can draw in dust and debris.
Ice on the intake or filter from visible moisture below 0°C.

quiz.q: On a warm humid day you are descending at low power. Which statement is correct?
o: Carb ice can still form and descent power is the highest-risk setting
Carb ice only forms in cloud
Only fuel-injected engines are at risk
quiz.why: Serious carb ice has been shown with air above 25°C and humidity as low as 30%, especially at descent power.

quiz.q: Your fixed-pitch propeller RPM drops slightly and airspeed falls. What do you do first?
o: Open the throttle and ignore it
Apply carb heat and accept some rough running while it clears
quiz.why: Select heat and keep it on. The engine may run rough as ice melts.

quiz.q: At the power check, carb heat on gives a typical drop of:
quiz.why: A drop of about 75 to 100 RPM, or 3 to 5 inches of MP, is expected. A rise afterwards suggests ice was cleared.

quiz.q: Why should you apply carb heat before closing the throttle in the descent?
o: Ice is much more likely at reduced power
quiz.why: Induction ice is far more likely at low power, so heat goes on before power comes off.

quiz.q: Which engine type can suffer intake icing but not carb icing?
quiz.why: Fuel-injected engines have no carburettor but can ice at the intake or filter, so check alternate air.

quiz.q: At about 300 ft on final many aircraft call for carb heat to be:
o: Selected cold ready for a go-around
quiz.why: Cold heat gives full power if you go around, but follow the AFM.
